overview.title: 📖 Overview: Redemption Values and a Sermon on Decline
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 30a–30b
overview.hebrewSource: מְכָרָהּ לָרִאשׁוֹן בְּמָנֶה, וּמָכַר רִאשׁוֹן לַשֵּׁנִי בְּמָאתַיִם, אֵינוֹ מְחַשֵּׁב אֶלָּא עִם הָרִאשׁוֹן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf works out exactly which sale price governs when a field is redeemed after passing through two buyers, and finds — through a verbal analogy to the redemption of a Hebrew slave — that the Torah always favors the seller by calculating at whichever value is lower. That leniency triggers Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina's famous, sobering sermon tracing a person's descent from selling movable goods all the way down to selling himself into slavery to idol worship, and Abaye's insistence that the Torah still eases his redemption despite his sins. A final new mishna returns to practical law: an ordinary field sale carries strict redemption rules that consecrated property redemption does not.

slides.title: 📉 A Field Resold: Which Price Governs Redemption?
slides.subtitle: New mishna, with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda offering different readings
rows: Sold to buyer #1 for 100, buyer #1 resold to buyer #2 for 200
'To the man to whom he sold it' (Lev. 25:27) — Rebbi's reading
Sold to buyer #1 for 200, buyer #1 resold to buyer #2 for 100
'To the man' — the man currently holding it
Same buyer throughout; field appreciated from 100 to 200
R' Dostai ben Yehuda: 'he returns the remainder' — of the money in his hand
Same buyer throughout; field depreciated from 200 to 100
R' Dostai ben Yehuda: the remainder of the land's value

callout.label: Common thread:
callout.text: Both readings agree on the underlying principle: the law always favors the seller with whichever number is lower. The practical difference between them emerges only in a case where the value rose, then fell, then rose again.

slides.title: ⚖️ Proving the Torah's Leniency in Redemption
slides.subtitle: Why favor the lower value rather than the higher one?

nodes.content: ❓ Why assume the verses favor the seller (lower value) rather than the buyer (higher value)?
🔗 Gezeirah shava: 'redemption' (geulah) here is linked to 'redemption' used for a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile
📜 There too: if his value rose, he redeems himself at the ORIGINAL (lower) price; if it fell, at the CURRENT (lower) price — proven from 'the money of his purchase' vs. 'according to his years'

✅ Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the phrase 'in the years' (not just 'years') signals this is about value fluctuating during those years, not about counting years themselves — Rav Yosef calls this reading 'as true as if given at Sinai'

slides.title: 🌀 Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina's Sermon: The Slippery Slope
slides.subtitle: One violation of Shvi'it/Jubilee halakhot triggers a chain of ruin — each drawn from an adjacent verse

steps.content: 1️⃣ Trades in Sabbatical-year produce → eventually sells his movable property
2️⃣ Doesn't feel remorse → eventually sells his ancestral fields
3️⃣ Still doesn't register it → eventually sells his house in a walled city
4️⃣ Still nothing → borrows money with interest, then sells his daughter, then finally sells HIMSELF — to a fellow Jew, then a stranger, then a ger toshav, then even into service of idol worship

callout.label: Rav Huna's principle behind the shift in language:
callout.text: The sermon says 'he does not feel remorse' at first, then 'consciousness does not come to him' later — reflecting Rav Huna's teaching that repeating a sin twice makes it feel, to the sinner, as though it were permitted.

slides.title: 🪨 Should His Redemption Still Be Made Easy?
slides.subtitle: Given how far he's fallen by his own choices, why help him at all?

lines.speaker: A challenger
lines.text: Since it's entirely his own sins that brought him this low — even into idol worship — shouldn't we be STRICT about his redemption, not lenient?

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: No — the Merciful One is explicitly gentle with a Hebrew slave: he must be housed, fed, and given drink 'with you,' as an equal. 'One who acquires a Hebrew slave acquires a master for himself.'

lines.speaker: Challenger
lines.text: But the school of Rabbi Yishmael itself asks: since he sold himself even to idol worship, why not 'throw a stone after the fallen' and abandon him?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: The verse answers its own question: 'he shall have a perpetual right of redemption' — so that he isn't assimilated among the nations. Leniency in redemption stands, regardless of how he got there.

slides.title: 🚫 New Mishna: Redeeming From a Private Buyer vs. From Hekdesh
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon explains why consecrated-field redemption is actually easier

boxes.title: Redeeming From an Ordinary Buyer
items: May NOT sell a distant field to redeem a nearby one
May NOT sell a low-quality field to redeem a high-quality one
May NOT borrow money to redeem
May NOT redeem in installments (half now, half later)

boxes.title: Redeeming From the Temple Treasury
items: ALL of these methods are permitted
R' Shimon's reasoning: a private-sale field is 'empowered' — it returns to the seller automatically at the Jubilee even unredeemed
So its redemption process is restricted; a consecrated field is 'weakened' (goes to the priests if unredeemed), so its redemption is eased instead

summary.principle: The Torah consistently favors the seller in redemption calculations — always the lower of two values, proven by analogy to a Hebrew slave's redemption — while a homiletic chain warns how easily poverty snowballs from minor violations to utter ruin; and practical law makes redeeming a privately sold field far more restrictive than redeeming one from the Temple treasury, precisely because the private field enjoys the built-in protection of automatic return at the Jubilee.

flowSteps.content: 📉 A twice-sold field's redemption price follows the first sale (or last, if reversed); same-buyer cases follow whichever value is lower
⚖️ Proven lenient via gezeirah shava to a Hebrew slave's redemption, which also always favors the lower value

columns.content: 🌀 R' Yosei bar Ḥanina: unchecked minor violations spiral into selling everything, even oneself
🪨 Even a self-sold slave still gets the Torah's lenient redemption terms

flowSteps.content: 🚫 A private field sale restricts redemption methods (no distant-swap, no borrowing, no installments); hekdesh redemption allows all of them
🎓 Key Principle: the law's leniency or strictness tracks precisely who already holds the structural advantage — the seller, the slave, or the Temple treasury

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reading of the new mishna, if a field was sold to a first buyer for 100 dinars, who then resold it to a second buyer for 200 dinars, at what price is the field redeemed?
o: 200 dinars, the most recent price
150 dinars, an average of the two
100 dinars, the price of the FIRST sale
The field cannot be redeemed once resold
quiz.e: Rebbi derives from 'to the man to whom he sold it' (Lev. 25:27) that when the price decreased with resale, redemption is calculated according to the first buyer's original price of 100 dinars.

quiz.q: What underlying principle does the Gemara prove via a gezeirah shava between a field's redemption and a Hebrew slave's redemption?
o: That both must be redeemed with borrowed money
That both are always calculated using whichever value is LOWER, favoring the seller/slave
That both require exactly two witnesses
That both can only be redeemed during the Jubilee Year
quiz.e: The Gemara links the word 'redemption' in both contexts to show that just as a Hebrew slave's redemption price is always calculated at the lower of his original or current value, so too is a field's redemption price.

quiz.q: In Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina's sermon, what marks the escalating stages of a person's financial and moral decline?
o: He immediately sells himself into slavery without warning signs
He progresses from selling movable goods, to fields, to his house, to borrowing with interest, to selling his daughter, and finally to selling himself into slavery
He only ever loses his house and nothing else
The stages are unrelated to Sabbatical Year or Jubilee violations
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina traces a step-by-step decline, each tied to an adjacent Torah verse, from trading in Sabbatical-year produce all the way down to selling oneself into servitude — even to idol worship.

quiz.q: How does Abaye respond to the challenge that a self-sold slave (who even sold himself to idol worship) should face STRICTER redemption terms because of his own sins?
o: He agrees and imposes stricter terms
He cites that the Torah requires the slave be treated as an equal ('with you') and that the verse itself guarantees him a perpetual right of redemption so he isn't assimilated among the nations
He says the slave has no right to redemption at all
He argues the question is irrelevant since slavery no longer exists
quiz.e: Abaye points to the Torah's explicit gentleness toward a Hebrew slave and to the verse promising him 'a perpetual right of redemption,' explaining that leniency stands specifically so he won't be lost among the gentiles, regardless of how he got there.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon in the new mishna, why can one redeem a Temple-treasury (hekdesh) field by borrowing money or paying in installments, when neither is allowed for a privately sold field?
o: Because hekdesh fields are worth less money

Because a privately sold field already has the built-in advantage of automatically returning to the seller at the Jubilee if unredeemed, so its redemption process is restricted; a consecrated field lacks that advantage (it goes to the priests instead), so its redemption is eased
Because Temple treasurers are permitted to lend money
There is no real reason; it is a fixed decree with no logic given
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon explains the Torah balances the scales: since an unredeemed privately-sold field reverts to the seller anyway at the Jubilee, its redemption is deliberately restricted; since an unredeemed consecrated field is LOST to the priests instead, its redemption is deliberately made easier.
